God, the Master, is present in water and on land;
whichever way I turn my eyes, the Knower of hearts is there.
He himself has made his devotion firm (in me).
O my brother, the writ of the past has come to me.
Whomever (God) blesses with grace, for him all is made complete;
Kabir's Master is the One who raises up the poor.
331.3: Sutak is in the water, Sutak is on the land; Sutak keeps arising (everywhere).
At birth there is Sutak, and at death again Sutak; by Sutak the people are ruined.
Tell me, O pandit, who is pure?
Dwell on such knowledge, O my friend.
In the eyes is Sutak, in speech is Sutak, and Sutak is in the ears;
rising or sitting, Sutak clings (to one); Sutak falls on the kitchen (too).
Everyone knows the way to be caught; the way to get free, hardly one (knows).
Says Kabir: one who reflects on Ram in the heart is not touched by Sutak.
331.4: Raag Gauri, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji.
Settle one dispute (for me), O Ram,
if you have any work for your servant.
Is this mind the greater, or he in whom the mind has come to trust?
Is Ram the greater, or one who has come to know Ram?
Is Brahma the greater, or the One who brought him forth?
Is the Veda the greater, or the source from which it came?
Says Kabir: I have grown uneasy (over this):
is the place of pilgrimage the greater, or the servant of the Lord?
331.5: Raag Gauri Cheti, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji.
Look, O brother: the storm of (divine) knowledge has come;
all the thatch of doubt has blown away; tied though it was by Maya, it does not stay.
The two posts of double-mindedness have fallen, the ridge-beam of attachment has snapped;
the roof-thatch of craving has come down to the earth, and the vessel of evil counsel is smashed.
In the rain that pours down after the storm, your servant is soaked through.
Says Kabir: light filled my mind when I recognised the risen sun.
332.1: Raag Gauri Cheti, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji.
Ik Oankar: God is One, the all-pervading Creator, realised through the True Guru's grace.
(Some) neither listen to the Lord's praise nor sing of the Lord's virtues,
yet by talk alone they pull the sky down.
What is there to say to such people?
Those whom God has kept outside devotion: let us always stay wary of them.
They themselves give no one even a palmful of water,
yet they slander the one who brought the Ganga down (to earth).
Sitting or rising, they walk in crooked ways;
lost themselves, they bring others to ruin too.
Apart from evil talk they know nothing else;
they do not heed even what Brahma says.
Lost themselves, they lead others astray too;
they set fire to the house and sleep inside it.
They mock others, though they are one-eyed themselves;
332.2: Raag Gauri Bairagan, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji.
Ik Oankar: God is One, the all-pervading Creator, realised through the True Guru's grace.
No one honours his forebears while they live; once they are dead, people have the shraadh done for them.
Tell me, how can the poor forebears receive (that food)? Crows and dogs eat it.
Let someone tell me what well-being is.
Crying for well-being, well-being, the world perishes; how can well-being come at all?
They shape gods and goddesses from clay, and before them offer up a life.
Such are those called your forebears: they take nothing by asking for it with their own mouths.
They kill the living and worship the lifeless; at the last hour it will weigh heavy (on them).
They have not known the state that Ram's Name brings; the worldly are drowned in fears.
They worship gods and goddesses and stay unsteady; the Supreme Lord they have not known.
Says Kabir: they have not remembered the Lord who has no lineage (Akul); they cling to the poison (of Maya).
332.3: Raag Gauri, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji.
One who dies while living, and, so dying, lives again, is thus absorbed in Sunn (the stillness where no worldly thought stirs):
amid the black stain of Maya one dwells in the Niranjan, and is not cast into the world-ocean again.
O my Ram, let the milk be churned in this way:
keep the mind steady through the Guru's teaching; this is how the Amrit is drunk.
By the Guru's arrow (of the Word) the adamant-hard (veil of illusion) has been pierced, and the state of light has shone forth;
the illusion of the rope (taken for a snake) in the darkness of Shakti (Maya) is ended, and the dwelling is fixed, unmoving, in the home of Shiv (the Lord, the source of good).
She (Maya) has pierced this world, O brother, drawing her bow without an arrow;
the wind tosses the kite about in all ten directions, but (my) string has stayed tied in loving attention.
In the state of unman the mind is absorbed in Sunn; duality and evil-mindedness have fled.
Says Kabir: I have seen a wonder known from within; my attention is fixed on Ram's Name.
333.1: Raag Gauri Bairagan, Tipade of Bhagat Kabir Ji.
As the wind (of the mind) is turned back, the six chakras are pierced, and the attention falls in love with Sunn.
He neither comes nor goes, neither dies nor is born: seek him, O bairagi.
O my mind, the mind itself, turned back (from the world), has merged (in the Lord).
By the Guru's grace the understanding has become other; else (it) was a stranger (to the Lord).
The near grows far, and the far grows near again, for one who has known (the Lord) as he truly is.
It is like a syrup made from sugar-candy: only one who has drunk it knows (its taste).
To whom can the tale of you, beyond the qualities (nirgun), be told? Rare is one so discerning.
Says Kabir: whoever has put fire to the fuse has seen a flash to match.
333.2: Raag Gauri, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji.
There, there is neither rain nor sea, neither sun nor shade; there, nothing is created or dissolved.
Neither life nor death, pain nor pleasure touches (one) there; Sunn and Samadhi, neither of the two, is there.
The tale of Sahaj cannot be told; it is unlike any other:
it goes on no scale, and is never used up; it seems neither light nor heavy.
Below and above, neither of the two is there; neither night nor day is there.
Water is not there, nor wind, nor fire either; there the True Guru abides.
The Lord, beyond reach and beyond the senses, dwells there unbroken; by the Guru's grace he is found.
Says Kabir: I am a sacrifice to my Guru; let us stay joined in the Sat Sangat.
333.3: Raag Gauri, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji.
Sin and virtue, a pair of oxen, have been bought; the breath has been laid out as capital;
within the body the sack is filled with craving: in this way the caravan (of laden oxen) has been bought.
Such a master-merchant is our Ram:
he has made the whole world a banjara (a travelling trader).
Lust and anger, the two, have become toll-collectors; the mind's waves are the robbers on the road;
the five elements, joining together, settle the toll, and the caravan has crossed to the far side.
Says Kabir: listen, O Sants, this is how it has now turned out:
climbing the steep pass, one ox has tired, and has gone off, throwing down its load.
333.4: Raag Gauri, a Panchpada of Bhagat Kabir Ji.
In the parents' home there are but four days; to the in-laws' home (the soul-bride) must go.
The blind world, foolish and childish, does not know this.
Tell me: the bride stands still in her workaday wrap (dadia),
and the guests have come to the house: those come to take her away in the muklava have arrived.
That little well that is seen: who is it lowering the rope into it?
The rope has broken along with the pitcher, and the water-carrier has risen and gone.
If the Master becomes kind and shows grace, (the soul-bride) accomplishes her own task;
then she is known as a happy wife, (when) she reflects on the Guru's Shabad.
All (the world) wanders bound by its past deeds: reflect, and see.
What is to be said to her? What can the poor thing do?
Without hope she has risen and gone; her mind finds no steadiness to hold.
Stay at the Lord's feet; run to his refuge, O Kabir.
334.1: Raag Gauri, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji.
Yogis say: yoga is good and sweet, there is nothing else, O brother.
The shaven ascetics, the shorn sannyasis, and those who cry the one word (Alakh): these all say they have attained siddhi.
Without the Lord, the blind wander lost in doubt;
those to whom I go to get myself released are themselves bound in many nooses.
(The soul) merges back into that from which it sprang only when this way (of pride) is forgotten:
these all say: we are pandits, men of virtue, warriors, givers; we alone are great.
Only the one whom (the Lord) gives understanding understands; without understanding, how can one live?
(When) the True Guru is met, the darkness ends; in this way the ruby (of the Name) is found.
Casting off the vices to left and right, let us hold fast to the state of (union with) the Lord.
Says Kabir: the mute has eaten molasses; asked about it, what can he say?
334.2: Raag Gauri Poorbi, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji.
Ik Oankar: God is One, the all-pervading Creator, realised through the True Guru's grace.
Where once there was something, nothing remains; nor are the five elements there.
Ida, Pingala and Sukhmana: O man, where have these flawed (practices) gone?
The thread is broken, the sky (the Tenth Gate) has perished; where has the one who spoke in you been absorbed?
This doubt troubles me night and day; no one explains it to me.
Where the universe (was beheld), the body is not there; nor is the mind, the maker (of it all), there.
The Joiner is ever detached; in whom, then, can this (speaker) be said to be?
(The body) is not held together by joining, nor broken apart by breaking, until its time to perish comes.
Who is whose master, and who whose servant? Who will go to whom?
Says Kabir: (my) attention stays fixed (there) where (the Lord) dwells day and night.
His secret he alone truly knows; he is forever imperishable.
334.3: Raag Gauri, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji.
Attention (fixed on the Lord) and remembrance (of him) are the earrings in my two ears; true knowledge (of him) is the patched coat I wear.
My seat, where I sit, is in the cave of Sunn; to be free of (worldly) imaginings is my path.
O my King, I am a bairagi yogi;
I neither die, nor grieve, nor know separation.
Through all the realms and the universe (sounds) my horn (singi); the whole world is my pouch for ashes.
My trance has set in: the three qualities are turned back, and one is freed even while living amid the world's spread.
Mind and breath, the two, I have made the gourds, and (the Lord) of all the ages the stem (of my kingri);
the string has grown steady and will not break; the kingri sounds, unstruck (Anhad).
Hearing it, the mind is wholly absorbed, and Maya's shaking does not reach it.
Says Kabir: there is no birth again for the bairagi who has played (this game) and departed.
335.1: Raag Gauri, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji.
Nine yards, ten yards and twenty-one yards: one full warp has been stretched (on the loom of the body);
(in it are) sixty threads and nine joined pieces, and a weft of seventy-two (threads) is added over and above.
Maho, (the mind's craving,) has gone to have (this cloth) woven;
when (his true) home is left, the weaver (the soul) sets out (into birth).
It is not measured in yards, nor weighed on scales, (yet each day) its sizing is two and a half seers;
if it does not get its sizing in good time, it raises a quarrel within the house itself.
For a stay of a few days (the soul) turns against the Master; how will this hour come (again)?
The troughs are left behind, the bobbins stay wet, and the weaver departs in vexation.
The bobbin is empty, no thread comes out, and the beam stays tangled (in the threads) no more.
Says Kabir, teaching her: poor wretch, leave this spread (of entanglement) and stay here.
335.2: Raag Gauri, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji.
When one's light has merged in the One, does (a separate self) remain? It does not.
The one in whose heart the Naam does not spring up, that person bursts (with ego) and dies.
O dark and beautiful Ram, my dear one,
my mind is fixed on you.
When the Saadh (the Guru) is met, fulfilment is attained, whether one lives in yoga or in the world's enjoyments.
When the two (the Guru and the disciple) meet, the work bears fruit: union through the Name of Ram.
People take this for a song, but it is reflection on God (Brahm),
like the teaching given in Kashi to a man at the hour of his death.
Whoever sings or hears the Name of the Lord with the mind attuned,
says Kabir: there is no doubt; in the end he attains the supreme state.
335.3: Raag Gauri, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji.
All who make (such) efforts have drowned; (these efforts) have not carried (them) across the world-ocean, O brother.
Performing rites, religious duties and many disciplines, (their) mind is burnt up by the ego-intellect, O brother.
The Master is the giver of breath and food; why have you forgotten him from your mind, O brother?
(Human) birth is a diamond, a priceless ruby; you have lost it in exchange for a cowrie shell, O brother.
Through wandering, craving, thirst and hunger cling to you; you have not reflected in your heart, O brother.
Intoxicated, robbed by pride within your mind, you have not held the Guru's Shabad (within), O brother.
Greedy for tastes, driven by the pleasures of the senses, you take the heady relish of vices, O brother.
Those whose destiny holds good deeds join the Sants; (the Lord) saves them, as wood carries iron across, O brother.
Running, wandering through species and births, I am weary; now, worn by suffering, I have given up, O brother.
Says Kabir: on meeting the Guru (I found) the supreme relish; loving devotion has carried (me) across, O brother.
335.4: Raag Gauri, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji.
Like the she-elephant built on a frame (to trap an elephant), O crazed mind, is the play the Lord of the world has staged:
through the lure of lust the elephant is caught, O crazed mind, and bears the goad upon his head.
Keep clear of vices and merge in the Lord; understand this, O crazed mind.
You have not become fearless and worshipped the Lord, O crazed mind; you have not taken hold of the ship of Ram.
The monkey stretched out his hand and grabbed a fistful of grain, O crazed mind;
then the worry of getting free fell on him, O crazed mind, and he was made to dance at the door of house after house.
As the parrot is caught by the nalini, O crazed mind, such is the dealing of Maya.
As is the colour of safflower (bright, and soon gone), O crazed mind, so is this expanse spread out.
There are many tiraths to bathe at, O crazed mind, and many gods to worship;
says Kabir: (by these) there is no release, O crazed mind; release lies in the service of the Lord.
336.1: Raag Gauri, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji.
Fire does not burn it, wind does not blow it away, no thief comes near it:
gather the wealth of the Name of Ram; that wealth goes nowhere.
My wealth is Madho, Gobind, who upholds the earth; this, it is said, is wealth of the finest kind.
The peace that lies in serving God, Gobind, is not to be had in kingship.
For this wealth Shiv and Sanak and his brothers searched, and became detached (from the world).
With Mukand in the mind and Narayan on the tongue, the noose of Jam does not fall (on one).
The Guru has given (me) wealth truly my own, divine knowledge and devotion; with good understanding (my) mind is fixed on it.
(It is) water for the burning, a pillar for the running mind; the fear of doubt's bonds has fled.
Says Kabir: O you drunk with desire, reflect and see in your heart:
your house holds lakhs and crores of horses and elephants; my house holds the one Murari.
336.2: Raag Gauri, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji.
As the monkey, in his greed, would not let go the fistful of chickpeas in his hand,
(so) whatever deeds were done in greed, those in turn fell around (one's) neck.
Without devotion, life has gone in vain;
without the Saadh Sangat and the worship of the Lord (Bhagvan), the True One has abided nowhere.
As a flower blossoms in the wilderness and no one takes its fragrance,
so (beings) wander through many species, and are slain by death again and again.
This wealth, youth, sons and wife, which (the Lord) gave (only) to behold:
those who stick fast in these very things and are entangled, the senses have pulled them along.
The passing of life is a fire, the body a house of straw; on all four sides this is how it is built.
Says Kabir: to cross the terrifying ocean, I have taken refuge with the True Guru.
336.3: Raag Gauri, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji.
The water (the father's seed) is unclean, the clay (the mother's blood) is red;
of this clay a puppet has been put together.
I am nothing, and nothing is mine;
body, wealth and all (its) life-sap are yours, O Gobind.
Into this clay the breath (of life) has entered,
and (on it) a false show has been put together and set going.
Someone has amassed five lakh (in wealth);
at the last hour the pitcher (of the body) broke.
Says Kabir: the foundation that has been raised
is destroyed in an instant, O proud one.
337.1: Raag Gauri, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji.
O my soul, let me repeat (the Name of) Ram in such a way,
as Dhru and Prahlad repeated (the Name of) the Lord.
O merciful to the meek, trusting in you
I have put all my family aboard the boat.
When it pleases him, he makes (them) obey his Hukam,
By the Guru's grace such understanding has entered (me)
that coming and going (in births) again has ended.
on this shore and the far shore, know the One alone in all.
337.2: Raag Gauri 9, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji.
When, leaving the womb, (a being) came into the world,
as soon as the air (of the world) touched it, it forgot the Master.
O my soul, sing the praises of the Lord.
In the womb it practised austerity, hanging head down;
then it lived (unharmed) in the fire of the belly.
Wandering through the eighty-four lakh forms of life, it has come (to this birth);
if it misses this time, there is no place or resting place (for it).
(a being) is seen coming, but its going is not known.
337.3: Raag Gauri Poorbi, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji.
Let us not crave a dwelling in heaven, nor fear a dwelling in hell;
what is to be will be; let us not build hopes in the mind.
Let us sing the praises of the dear Lord (Ramaiya),
from whom the supreme treasure is obtained.
What use is chanting, what use austerity and self-discipline, what use fasting, what use bathing (at tiraths),
as long as the way of loving devotion to the Lord (Bhagvan) is not known?
Let us not be elated at the sight of prosperity, nor weep at the sight of adversity;
as prosperity is, so is adversity: what the Creator has ordained comes to pass.
Says Kabir: now I have come to know (that the Lord dwells) within the hearts of the Sants;
those servants are good in (their) service in whose hearts Murari dwells.
337.4: Raag Gauri, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji.
O mind, no one is yours; do not drag (others') burden onto yourself.
Like the birds' night-roost in a tree, such is this world.
I have drunk the relish of Ram, O brother,
through which relish all other relishes are forgotten.
Why weep when others die, when one's own self does not stay fixed?
Whatever is born will perish; let misfortune weep in grief, not I.
(My soul) is absorbed in the One from whom it sprang, drinking (this relish) in the company of the brave (devotees).
Says Kabir: I have kept (Ram) in my mind; remembering Ram, (I have found) detachment.
337.5: Raag Gauri, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji.
The woman watches the road; her eyes brimming (with tears), she heaves deep sighs;
her heart is not soothed, her foot does not stir, in the hope of the sight of the Lord.
that I may soon meet my beloved Ram.
Says Kabir: to attain the state of (true) life, let devotion to the Lord be practised;
the Name of Narayan is the one support: let the tongue repeat Ram.
338.1: Raag Gauri 11, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji.
(He) around whom grew thick clumps of tulsi (holy basil), who sang with love in the midst of the woods:
beholding his form, the milkmaid was enchanted (and said): do not leave me to come or go (elsewhere).
My mind is fixed on your feet, O Saringdhar (the Lord who bears the bow);
he alone meets you who is greatly fortunate.
In Brindaban, he who steals the mind, the enchanting Krishna, grazes the cows;
O Saringdhar, (I am the one) whose Master you are; my name is Kabir.
338.2: Raag Gauri Poorbi 12, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji.
Many have put on ample (holy) robes; what (comes) of living in the forest?
What came of it, O man, if gods were worshipped with incense? What, if (the body) was knowingly drowned in water?
O soul, you will depart: this I know.
Understand the Unmanifest (Lord), O ignorant one.
Whatever I look upon, I do not see again; (yet you) are wrapped up in Maya.
The learned, the meditative, the great preachers: this whole world is (caught in Maya's) entanglement.
Says Kabir: lacking the Name of the one Ram, this world goes blind in Maya.
338.3: Raag Gauri 12, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji.
O mind, you whom this Maya holds to punishment, give up doubt and dance in the open.
What warrior is he who shrinks from the battle he faces? What sati is she who gathers up her pots?
Give up wavering, O crazed mind;
now that the sindhaura has been taken in hand, fulfilment comes only by burning and dying.
Seized by lust, anger and Maya, in this way the world is ruined.
Says Kabir: I will not forsake Ram, the King, the highest of all the high.
338.4: Raag Gauri 13, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji.
I bear your command upon my head; I do not turn round to weigh it.
You are the river, you are the boatman; from you alone comes deliverance.
O man, take up the worship (of the Lord),
whether the Master shows anger or love.
Your Name is my support, as the flower lives in water.
Says Kabir: I am the slave of your house; keep me alive or kill me, as you please.
338.5: Raag Gauri, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji.
(You say that) Nand grew very weary, wandering among the beings of the eighty-four lakh forms of life,
and for (his) devotion (God) took birth (in his house): great was the fortune of that poor man.
You who say, O brother, that (God became) the son of Nand: whose son, then, was that Nand?
When there was neither earth nor sky, nor the ten directions, where then was this Nand?
He falls into no affliction (of birth and death) and enters no womb, the One whose Name is Niranjan.
Such is Kabir's Lord and Master: he has neither mother nor father.
339.1: Raag Gauri, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji.
Let people slander me, slander me, slander me (as much as they like);
to (the Lord's) servant, slander is truly dear;
If slander comes, one goes to Baikunth,
and the treasure of the Naam is made to dwell in the mind.
If slander comes while the heart is pure,
Whoever slanders me is my friend;
my mind stays on the slanderer.
The (true) slanderer is the one who holds back slander (of me);
the slanderer wants my life (to be made good).
Slander of me is love and affection (to me);
For the servant Kabir, slander is the best (of things):
the slanderer has drowned, and I have crossed over.
339.2: O Ram, the King, so fearless are you; you are the boat that carries (beings) across, O Sovereign Ram.
When I was (in my ego), you were not (in me); now you are, and I am not.
Now we two, you and I, are one; beholding the One alone, my mind is at rest.
When (pride in my own) cleverness held sway, what strength (of spirit) was there? Now (pride in) cleverness and strength no longer holds.
Says Kabir: (the Lord) has taken away my (proud) intellect; my intellect is changed, and (I) have reached fulfilment.
339.3: Raag Gauri, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji.
Of six rings (the five elements and the mind) the little room (of the body) has been built, and an incomparable thing has been placed within it;
the breath of life has been made its lock and key; in making it, (the Creator) took no time.
Now stay awake, O mind, O brother:
heedless, (you) have wasted your life; the thief goes in and plunders the house.
Five watchmen (the senses) stay at the door, but there is no trusting them.
Keep (the Lord) in mind, stay alert in your thought, and then you will receive the light, the brightness (within).
The soul-bride who, seeing the nine houses (of the body), went astray has not found the incomparable thing.
Says Kabir: when the nine houses are plundered (their hold stripped away), in the tenth the essence (of the Lord) is found abiding.
339.4: Raag Gauri, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji.
O mother, I have known no other, none besides (the Lord):
my breath of life dwells in him whose virtues Shiv and Sanak and the others sing.
By the wisdom the Guru has imparted, the heart is lit, and attention is fixed in the realm of the sky (the Tenth Gate).
The diseases of the senses' pleasures, fear and bonds have fled; in its own home the mind has known peace.
(My) good understanding is in love with the One; knowing God and trusting him, (I) bring no second into my mind.
The mind's cravings given up, there is (within) the fragrance of sandalwood, and pride has dwindled.
The servant who sings and meditates on the Master's praise: in him God makes his dwelling.
Great is the fortune of one in whose mind (God) has come to dwell; the highest destiny is on his forehead.
Shakti (Maya) cut away, the Sahaj of Shiv (the Lord) has shone forth, and (the mind) has merged in the One alone.
Says Kabir: in meeting the Guru there is supreme peace; the wandering has ended, and the mind is at rest.
340.1: Raag Gauri Poorbi, Bavan Akhri: the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji.
There is one God, Ik Oankar, the One who pervades all and is ever the same; his Name is Sat (the One who truly is); he is the Creator, the Being who dwells in all, realised by the Guru's grace.
Fifty-two letters (serve) the three worlds; all things are (held) in these alone.
These letters will wear away; those letters (that could tell of union with the Lord) are not among them.
340.2: Where there is speech, letters come in;
where (the state) beyond speech is, there the mind itself does not remain.
In speech and in the speechless alike, he alone is;
(yet) as he truly is, so no one can perceive him.
340.3: If I find the Unfindable, what can I say (of him)? And if I do speak, what good is it?
As the banyan lies in its seed, so he pervades (all), the One whose spread is the three worlds.
340.4: Seeking the Unfindable, (my) sense of separateness has been destroyed, and I have grasped something of (his) mystery.
With separateness overturned, the mind is pierced (with the Lord), and (I) have found the One who cannot be broken or pierced.
340.5: The Turk (the Muslim) is known by the tariqat, the Hindu by the Vedas and the Puranas;
(but) for the mind's instruction, one should read something of (divine) wisdom.
340.6: Oankar (the all-pervading Lord) I have known as the Origin (of all);
the one whom he writes and erases I do not accept (as God).
then, having perceived him, (that one) is not destroyed.
340.7: Kaka: if I bring the ray (of the sun of wisdom) into the lotus (of the heart),
then in the light of the moon (of Maya) it does not close (again).
And if there I taste the nectar of the flower,
it is beyond telling: what can I say? What can I explain by speaking?
340.8: Khakha: (when) this mind comes into the hollow (of its own true self),
it does not leave the hollow to run off in the ten directions.
One who, knowing the Master, abides in forbearance
then becomes imperishable and attains the undying state.
340.9: Gaga: one who has recognised the Guru's word
lends no ear to any other talk.
He lives like a bird (unattached), and strays nowhere;
he takes hold of the Ungraspable (in his heart), and, holding him, keeps to the sky within (the Tenth Gate).
340.10: Ghagha: in every body he alone dwells;
when the pitcher (of the body) breaks, he is never lessened.
When one finds within that very body the ford (for crossing over),
why would he leave that ford and run into pathless ravines?
340.11: Nganga: restrain (the senses), love (the Lord), and cast out doubt.
Do not run away on seeing that (it seems) it cannot be done: this is the highest wisdom.
340.12: Chacha: (this world) that he has made is a vast picture;
leave the picture and keep the Painter in mind.
This is the snare: the picture is wondrous (and enticing);
leave the picture, and keep your mind on the Painter.
340.13: Chhachha: the Sovereign of the royal canopy is right here beside (you);
why not stay absorbed (in him)? Why not give up (other) hopes?
O mind, every moment I counsel you:
leaving him, where are you getting yourself bound?
340.14: Jaja: when one burns (the cravings of) the body while still alive,
burning away (the pride of) youth, he finds the (true) way (to live).
When, burning away (the sense of) mine and others', he lives on, enduring (all),
then he goes on (to the higher state) and finds the brightness of the (divine) Light.
341.1: Jhajha: one who (learned only) to be entangled, and never knew how to get free,
stayed hesitating, and was not accepted.
What (use) is it to wrangle and wrangle to instruct others?
By quarrelling, only quarrels are gained.
341.2: Nyanya: he dwells close by, in the heart; forsaking him, where do you go so far?
The One for whom I searched the world, I found close at hand.
341.3: Tatta: the hard ford (to the Lord) is within the heart itself;
why not open the doors (of Maya) and go into (the Lord's) mansion?
Seeing the Unmoving One, (the mind) does not waver and go elsewhere;
it stays clinging (to him), and in the heart comes to know him intimately.
341.4: Thattha: this (Maya) is deceiving water seen from afar (a mirage);
looking closely, again and again, I have made (my) mind steady.
The cheat who by cheating has swallowed the whole world:
by cheating that cheat, (my) mind has come to its place of rest.
341.5: Dadda: when (God's) fear arises, (worldly) fear goes;
in that fear (every other) fear is absorbed.
If one shrinks in fear from (God's) fear, then (worldly) fear clings again.
One who has (so) become fearless: whatever fear is in his heart runs away.
341.6: Dhaddha: (the Lord is) near; why search for (him) elsewhere?
In the very searching, the breath of life is spent.
When, having climbed Sumer and searched, (I) came back,
the One who built the fortress (of the body) I found within the fortress.
341.7: Nanna: the man who, engaged on the battlefield, holds firm,
who neither bows down (to the vices) nor goes along (with them):
his birth alone (the world) counts blessed,
(for he) slays the one (the mind) and leaves the many (vices) behind.
341.8: Tata: (the world-ocean) is uncrossable; it cannot be crossed,
(while) the body (with its senses) stays sunk in (the things of) the three worlds.
When the three worlds are absorbed within the body,
then essence (the soul) merges with essence (the Lord), and the True One is found.
341.9: Thatha: the depth of the Fathomless cannot be found;
he is fathomless, and this (mind) does not stay still.
On a little patch of ground it sets about (building great) towns,
and would hold up a mansion with no pillars at all.
341.10: Dada: all that is seen is bound to perish;
keep in your thought the One who is unseen, as he is.
When the key is turned in the Tenth Gate,
then one has the sight of the Merciful One.
341.11: Dhadha: the lower (the soul) finds its settlement in the Higher (the Lord),
(when) the lower dwells within the Higher.
When (the soul) leaves the lower (state) and comes up to the higher,
then the lower and the Higher meet, and peace is found.
341.12: Nana: night and day pass in watching (for the Lord);
watching, the eyes have grown red (with love).
When, watching and watching, (one) at last finds (him),
then the One watched for takes the watcher and unites (him with himself).
341.13: Pappa: the end of the One beyond whom there is none cannot be found;
one who has formed a bond with the Supreme Light
holds all five senses in check,
and puts away both sin and virtue.
341.14: Phapha: without flowering (into pride), the fruit (of life) comes;
if anyone perceives even a sliver of that fruit
and reflects on that sliver, he does not fall into the valley (of birth and death);
a sliver of that fruit tears apart all (attachment to) the body.
341.15: Babba: (as) a drop merges with a drop,
(so the soul) that comes to know (the Lord) even for a moment cannot be parted (from him again).
One who becomes (the Lord's) servant and holds fast to his worship,
becoming one who sings his praise, sees through the bonds (of Maya).
342.1: Bhabha: (the one who) has pierced the gulf (between him and the Lord) and joined (his mind to him),
now, with fear shattered, has come to trust (in the Lord).
The (Lord) who is outside (in all the world) he has known (dwelling) within;
(when) the secret was opened, he recognised the Master of the earth.
342.2: Mamma: holding fast to the Root (of all), the mind is won over (and stops wandering);
one who knows this secret comes to understand the mind.
When the mind is coming to meet (the Lord), let no one delay:
absorbed (in him), one finds the True (Lord).
342.3: Mamma: (one's real) task is with the mind; by disciplining the mind, success is won.
Says Kabir: (the dealing) is with the mind alone, with the mind; I have met no other like the mind.
342.4: This mind is Shakti (Maya), this mind is Shiv (the Lord, the giver of good);
this mind is what gives life to the body of five elements.
When (one) takes this mind in hand and dwells in the state of unman,
then he speaks of (the Lord who fills) the three worlds.
342.5: Yaya: if you would know (the way), destroy your evil-mindedness and bring the village of the body under your rule.
Locked in battle, if (you) do not run away, (only) then do you bear the name of hero.
342.6: Rara: (the one who) has known the relish (of Maya) as tasteless,
becoming free of (these) relishes, has recognised that relish (of the Name).
By giving up these relishes, that relish has been found;
(whoever) has drunk that nectar, this relish does not please (him).
342.7: Lala: if the mind fixes its attention (on the Lord) in such a way
that it goes nowhere else, it finds the Supreme, the True (Lord);
and if there it fixes the attention of love,
then it finds the Unfindable (Lord), and having found him, merges in his feet.
342.8: Vava: again and again remember Bisan (the Lord);
remembering Bisan, one does not come away defeated (in the game of life).
I am a sacrifice, a sacrifice, to the son of Bisan (his devotee) who sings his praise;
meeting Bisan, one finds the True (Lord) everywhere.
342.9: Vaava: him alone should we know; by knowing him, this (soul) becomes (one with him).
When this (soul) and that (Lord) meet, then, once met, no one can know them apart.
342.10: Sassa: search him out (and remember him) with all care;
hold (the mind) to the words by which the heart is won over (to the Lord).
When the heart is won over and love wells up,
there the King of the three worlds is (seen) filling all.
342.11: Khakha: if anyone sets out to search (for the Lord),
whoever finds (him) does not come (into birth) again.
If (one) understands the signs (of the Lord) and reflects (on his virtues),
then (he) is not long in crossing the world-ocean.
342.12: Sassa: she (the soul-bride) adorns the bed (of the heart) for her Husband Lord;
she alone, the friend, is rid of (her) doubt,
(who) has given up petty pleasure and gained the supreme bliss;
then this one is called the wife, and that one the Husband.
342.13: Haha: having come into (human) being, (one) has not known (the Lord) who truly is.
Only when (the certainty of his being) comes is the mind won over.
He surely is, if anyone could perceive it;
then (the soul) is he himself, and is no longer this (separate self).
342.14: All the world goes about crying, Let me take, let me take;
for its sake, great sorrow besets (them).
When (one) fixes his attention on the Husband of Lakshmi (the Lord),
sorrow is wiped out, and he finds every comfort.
342.15: Khakha: wasting and wearing away, many (lives) have gone by;
wasting and wearing away, (one) does not remember (the Lord) even now.
Now, if knowing (what) the world (is), the mind holds steady (in the Lord),
it finds a firm place there, (in the Lord) from whom it was parted.
343.1: (People) have brought the fifty-two letters and joined them together,
(but) they could not recognise the One Akhar (the Imperishable).
Kabir speaks the Shabad of the True (Lord);
one who is a (true) pandit abides in the direct experience (of the Lord).
For pandits (these letters) are a trade,
for the wise, (a means of) reflecting on the essence.
As the understanding is in one's heart,
Says Kabir: so will that one know.
343.2: Ik Oankar: God is One, the all-pervading Creator, realised through the True Guru's grace.
Raag Gauri, Thiti: the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji.
(People keep) the fifteen lunar days and the seven weekdays;
Says Kabir: (I sing the Lord, who has) neither a near shore nor a far one.
When seekers and Siddhas come to know his secret,
(they see that) he himself is the Creator, he himself the Lord of light.
343.3: Amavas: on the new-moon day, let go of the hopes (you set on fasts and rites);
remember Ram, the Knower of hearts.
(So) while yet alive you will reach the gate of liberation,
and the Shabad, known by direct experience, (will be) the finest essence of your own self.
343.4: One who is dyed with love for the lotus feet of Gobind,
by the grace of the Sant (the Guru) has become pure in mind; night and day he stays awake in the Kirtan of the Lord.
343.5: Pariva: reflect on (the virtues of) the Beloved,
who, bodiless and boundless, plays within every body.
The dread of death never eats away at (the one who reflects on him),
(for) he stays merged in the Primal Being.
343.6: Dutiya: (such a one) knows (the world) as made of two parts,
Maya and Brahm (God); (God) pervades along with all.
without lineage, the Niranjan stays ever the same.
343.7: Tritiya: one who brings the three (qualities of Maya) into balance
attains the supreme state, the source of bliss.
In the Saadh Sangat faith wells up (in him)
that outside and within there is always (the Lord's) light.
343.8: Chauthahi: keep hold of the fickle mind,
and never sit in the company of lust and anger.
He who is himself all in all, in the water and on the land:
(joined) to him, repeat the chant that is truly your own.
343.9: Panchai: (this world) is a spread of the five elements;
(in it) the business of the two, gold and woman, (goes on).
Rare is the one who drinks the nectar of love (for the Lord);
the pain of old age and death does not come (to him) again.
343.10: Chhath: the six wheels (the five senses and the mind) run in all six directions;
unless won over (to the Lord), they do not stay still.
Erase duality and hold fast to forbearance,
(and) do not suffer the torment of rituals and rites.
343.11: Saatain: know the Word (of the Guru) as true,
(and) take the all-pervading Lord (Atam Ram) to heart.
(So) doubt is cast off, sorrows are wiped away,
and in the pool of Sunn you will find peace.
343.12: Astami: the body is (made) of eight elements;
within it dwells the (Lord) without lineage, the King of the great treasure.
The one to whom the wisdom of the Guru, who has reached (him), tells this secret
turns back (from love of the body) and dwells in the Indestructible, the Impenetrable.
343.13: Naumi: discipline the nine doors (of the body),
and keep bound the desires of the mind that flow out (through them).
Forget greed, attachment and all (the vices);
(then) you will live through the ages and eat the fruit that never perishes.
344.1: Dasmi: there is bliss in all ten directions,
doubt departs, and Gobind is met,
who is the embodiment of light, the essence (of all), beyond compare,
stainless, without any stain; (there) is neither shade nor sunshine.
344.2: Ekadasi: if (the mind) runs in one direction (to the One),
then (one) does not come into the anguish of births again.
the (Lord) said to be far off is found close by.
344.3: Baras: twelve suns rise (within, as it were);
day and night the unstruck trumpets sound;
(one) sees the Master of the three worlds;
a wonder comes to pass: from a (mere) creature he becomes Shiv (one with the Lord).
344.4: Teras: (one who) on the thirteenth (day) tells of the Unreachable (Lord)
recognises (him) as the same, from below to above.
(For him) there is no low or high, no honour or dishonour:
344.5: in every hair (of them), dwells Murari (the Lord).
Fix your mind on truth and contentment,
(and) speak the words (that bring) the knowledge of Brahm (God).
344.6: Puniu: (as on the full-moon night) the moon is full in the sky,
(and all its) phases spread out, (so within) shines the light of Sahaj.
(The Lord) stays unmoving at the beginning, at the end and in between;
Kabir delights in (him), the ocean of peace.
344.7: Ik Oankar: God is One, the all-pervading Creator, realised through the True Guru's grace.
Raag Gauri, Vaar Sat (the seven days): the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji.
Again and again I sing the virtues of the Lord;
reaching the Guru, I find that secret of the Lord.
Aadit: (one who) makes a beginning of devotion,
and in the temple of the body holds desire in check,
(his) attention flows on unbroken, day and night;
then the unstruck flute plays in Sahaj.
Somvar: the Amrit of the moon (its cool peace) trickles (within);
the moment it is tasted, it takes away every poison.
Held back by the Bani, (the mind) stays at (the Lord's) door;
then the mind, intoxicated, becomes the drinker (of that Amrit).
Mangalvar: (one) draws a wall (around the mind),
and comes to know the ways of the five thieves (lust and the rest).
Do not leave (this) house and go outside,
or else the King (the Lord) will be sorely angered.
Budhvar: (one) brings the light (of the Name) to the intellect,
(and) makes the heart-lotus the dwelling of the Lord.
Meeting the Guru, (one) holds the two (the soul and the Lord) as one,
(and) takes the upturned lotus (of the heart) and sets it upright.
Brihaspati: (one) washes away the poison (of Maya),
(and) joins the three gods to the One.
(Those who live) in the trikuti, (the fretting of Maya,) are (swept along) there in the three rivers (of the three qualities);
day and night they do not wash away (their) sins.
Sukrit: one who makes good deeds his support climbs (the steep path of) this vow:
night and day he fights against his own self;
he keeps all five senses in check;
then the eye of duality never enters (him).
Thavar: (one) keeps it steady,
the little lamp of (the Lord's) light that (burns) in the heart;
outside and within, light shines;
then all (past) karma is destroyed.
As long as the heart leans on another,
so long is there no entering the mansion (of the Lord).
Remembering Ram, love for Ram takes hold;
Says Kabir: then every limb becomes pure.
345.1: Raag Gauri Cheti, the hymn of Bhagat Namdev Ji.
Ik Oankar: God is One, the all-pervading Creator, realised through the True Guru's grace.
O Lord, you carried even stones across (the sea);
why then should your servants, uttering the Name of Ram, not cross over?
You saved the courtesan, and Kubija who had no beauty; you saved Ajamal, sick with sin;
the hunter who struck (Krishna's) foot with his arrow: even such people were set free.
I am a sacrifice, again and again, to those who have uttered the Name of Ram.
Bidar, the son of a maidservant, (became) your servant, and Sudama too; to Ugrasain you gave the kingdom.
Without recitations, without austerities, without high birth, without good deeds: O Master of Namdev, even they crossed over.
345.2: Raag Gauri, Pade of Bhagat Ravidas Ji: Gauri Guareri.
There is one God, Ik Oankar, the One who pervades all and is ever the same; his Name is Sat (the One who truly is); he is the Creator, the Being who dwells in all, realised by the Guru's grace.
The company I keep is low, and this worry stays with me day and night;
my deeds are crooked, and my birth is lowly.
O Ram, Gusaiya (Master of the earth), you who are the life of my soul,
do not forget me; I am your servant.
Take away my distress, and make your servant one of good heart;
I will not let go of your feet, even if the strength of my body goes.
Says Ravidas: I have come into your keeping;
come and meet your servant soon; make no delay.
The city's name is Begampura (the town without sorrow);
in that place there is neither pain nor grief;
there is no anxiety there, no tax and no property;
no fear, no wrongdoing, no dread, no decline.
Now I have found a fine homeland to live in;
there, my brother, all is always well.
Its rule stands firm and lasting, for ever;
none there is second or third (in rank); all are alike.
It is ever peopled and renowned;
those who dwell there are rich and fulfilled.
They go about wherever they please;
they are intimates of the (Master's) palace, and no one holds them back.
Says Ravidas the Chamar (of the leather-working caste), who has been set free:
whoever lives in our city is our friend.
345.3: Ik Oankar: God is One, the all-pervading Creator, realised through the True Guru's grace.
Raag Gauri Bairagan, the hymn of Bhagat Ravidas Ji.
The mountain passes are very hard to cross, and the one ox I have is good for nothing;
I make one prayer to the beloved Lord (Ramaiya): O Murari, protect my capital.
Is there any trader of the Lord (to go along with me), O brother? My caravan is laden and on its way.
I am a trader of the Lord; my trade is in Sahaj;
The load I have taken on is the Lord's Name, my wealth; poison is the load the world has taken on.
O knowers of (the deeds of) this world and the next, write (about me) whatever idle stuff you like;
Jam's punishment does not touch me, for I have given up all entanglements.
As is the colour of safflower, so is this world;
the colour of my beloved Lord's (love) is the (fast) colour of madder, says Ravidas the Chamar.
346.1: Raag Gauri Poorbi, the hymn of Bhagat Ravidas Ji.
Ik Oankar: God is One, the all-pervading Creator, realised through the True Guru's grace.
As frogs fill a well and know nothing of any land, their own or another,
just so my mind is bewitched by Maya, and it can see nothing of this shore or the far one.
O Master of all the worlds, let me see you, if only for a moment.
My understanding has grown soiled, O Madhav (Lord); your state cannot be known (by me).
Have mercy, that my doubt may end; teach me, and give me right understanding.
Even the masters of yoga do not reach (the end of) your virtues; the telling of them has no limit.
Says Ravidas the Chamar: (I ask for your sight) for the sake of loving devotion.
346.2: Raag Gauri Bairagan, the hymn of Bhagat Ravidas Ji.
Ik Oankar: God is One, the all-pervading Creator, realised through the True Guru's grace.
(The scriptures say:) in Satjug (the way was) truth, in Treta sacrifices, in Duapar the rites of worship;
the three ages held firmly to these three; in Kalyug the Name alone is the support.
How then will (one) reach the far shore, O brother?
No one explains to me clearly
(the way) by which coming and going (birth and death) would end.
Religious duties are set out in many ways, and the whole world is seen performing them;
(but) by which deed is one set free, the deed whose practice brings complete fulfilment?
If one weighs the deeds enjoined and the deeds forbidden, hearing the Vedas and Puranas (only) raises doubt;
doubt dwells always in the heart; who (then) will take away the pride?
The outside (of the body) is washed with water, (but) within the heart are vices of many kinds;
in what way will (one) become pure? Such purity is like the way of the elephant (which bathes and then throws dust on itself).
As the whole world knows how night passes away when the sun gives its light,
and know that copper touched by the paaras takes no time to become gold,
(so,) if it is written on the forehead from before, one meets the Guru, the supreme paaras;
the mind, in the state of unman, meets (the Lord) within itself, and the adamant doors open.
Whoever, by the way of devotion, has made his understanding true, cutting away doubt, bonds and vices,
he alone, dwelling (in the Lord) in joy, meets him in the mind, reflecting on the One who is both with qualities and beyond them.
Many efforts at restraint are made, (yet) the noose of doubt does not go, however one tries to remove it;
loving devotion does not spring up (from them); therefore Ravidas has turned away from them.

8.1: Dharam Raj judges each soul by its deeds; Chitr and Gupt are, by tradition, the two recorders at his court who write down the deeds of every being.

Mach is the mortal world, between heaven and the netherworld. The jewels: by tradition, the fourteen jewels that came out of the ocean when it was churned. The sixty-eight places of pilgrimage are the tiraths held most holy in India.
The four sources of life (khaani): birth from the egg, from the womb, from sweat and from the earth.
9.1: The Siddhas are yogis held to have reached perfection; siddhi is attainment, the miraculous powers among it.
9.2: Kamjaat (low-born) and sanaat (counted outside the four castes) are not caste by birth here: the Guru says the low are those who forget the Master.
10.1: Rahraas: the provisions for a journey; for the journey of life, the Lord's praise. The evening bani, Rehras, takes its name from it.
10.2: Madho (maa, Maya or Lakshmi, and dhav, husband): a name of God.
The crane (koonj) flies hundreds of kos in winter, leaving her young behind.
The treasures: by tradition, the nine treasures (nidhis). The eighteen siddhis: the miraculous powers of yoga, eight of them (anima, laghima and the rest) the best known.
10.3: So Purakh, taken from the opening words of this shabad, is the heading of four shabads, which are read in Rehras, the evening bani.
Niranjan: nir (without) and anjan (collyrium, black stain); the One on whom the stain of Maya does not fall.
Ji, in nearly every line of this shabad, is a word of reverence for God.
ਜਨੁ ਨਾਨਕੁ (with the aunkar) is the subject: servant Nanak himself is the sacrifice; ਜਨ ਨਾਨਕ (without it) is an address, O servant Nanak, or, with a postposition understood, of servant Nanak.

The Simritis are the Hindu books of conduct and law, the Shastras the books of the six schools of philosophy; the six duties (khat karam) are a Brahmin's: to study and to teach, to perform sacrifice and to have it performed, to give alms and to receive them.
11.1: Sachiar: sach and alaya (abode), the abode of truth, God who ever abides.
ਸਭ ਤੇਰੀ ਤੂੰ ਸਭਨੀ ਧਿਆਇਆ: here ਤੂੰ means you as the object (ਤੈਨੂੰ), and ਸਭਨੀ means by all.
Vijog and sanjog: the powers of God's will that part beings and bring them together.
12.1: The saravarra is a lake, here the world: its water is the fire of craving and its mire attachment. Pankaj here is not the lotus but the mire (pank).
Bhaile and dubiale are past forms of an eastern dialect: has come to be, have drowned.
12.2: The first six lines counsel the soul; in the last four Nanak prays humbly to God on behalf of all beings.
12.3: Sohila is a song of joy and praise, like the wedding songs sung on the nights before a marriage. Five shabads stand under this name, recited at night before sleep.

Stanzas 3 and 4 draw on the wedding rites: the year and the day of the wedding (saaha) are fixed in writing, the invitation (paahucha) goes to the houses of kin, and the bride's friends gather to pour the oil and give their blessings. Here the wedding is death, when the soul-bride goes to her Husband Lord.
12.4: The six houses are the six schools (darshanas) of Indian philosophy: Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Sankhya, Yoga, Mimamsa and Vedanta; the six teachers are their founders: Gautama, Kanada, Kapila, Patanjali, Jaimini and Vyasa.

The units of time: a visa is the time of fifteen blinks of the eye, fifteen visas make a chasa; a ghari is about twenty-four minutes and a pahar about three hours; the lunar days (thitis) are the dates of the moon's calendar.
13.1: Aarti is the worship in which a platter of lamps, incense and flowers is waved before an image; in this shabad all of nature performs the Creator's aarti. Malaanalo (malaya + anila, wind) is the fragrant breeze from the sandalwood hills of Malaya in the south of India; the fly-whisk (chaur) is waved over one who is revered.
The Anhad (anāhata, unstruck) Shabad is the sound made by no striking: the divine music that sounds unbroken through all creation.
The saaring (papiha, the rain-bird) is said to drink only drops of rain, and to keep calling out for them.
13.2: The ਹੇ that ends every line is not an address (O) but an old form of ਹੈ, is: ਖੰਡਾ ਹੇ, has been broken; ਪੁਨੁ ਵਡਾ ਹੇ, is a great merit.
15.2: Chuhra (the sweeper) and chandal: castes that those who kept rules of touch counted unclean, like the dog and carrion; the Guru gives these names to greed, falsehood, cheating, slander and anger.
16.2: The thirty-six dishes: by tradition, the full count of a royal feast.
17.1: The sixty-eight places of pilgrimage: the tiraths held most holy in India; the tikka is the sacred mark worn on the brow.
18.2: Kamdhenu (dhenu, cow): the cow of heaven in the Puranas, held to grant whatever is asked of her. Murari (the foe of the demon Mur): a name of God.
The three qualities (gunas) of Maya: rajas, sattva and tamas, under which all deeds are done. Trikuti: the three furrows of a frowning brow, the mind's fretting.
20.3: Anhad (anahata, unstruck): sound that rings without being struck, unbroken; in Gurbani, the Shabad of God's praise that resounds within without a break.
Shiv and Shakti: the conscious spirit and Maya; their union makes the world of the three qualities.
21.1: In ਲੋੁਭਾਨੁ the letter ਲ carries two vowel signs (ੋ and ੁ); it is read lubhaan, to keep the metre of the line.
Saakat (Sanskrit shakta): a worshipper of Shakti (Maya); in Gurbani, one cut off from God and lost in Maya.
21.2: The four fires: cruelty, attachment, greed and anger.
23.1: The parents' home (peeaa) is this world; the in-laws' home (saahuraa) is the world beyond, where the soul-bride goes to her Husband Lord.
23.2: The kaul (lotus) opens to the sun; the kavia (water-lily) opens to the moon.
23.3: Saringpani: he who holds the bow Saarang, a name of Vishnu; here, God.

The twenty-seven: in its month the moon passes through twenty-seven nakshatras (lunar mansions), and Brahmanical texts set a gift for each. The three junctures: dawn, noon and dusk, the times of the sandhya prayers. The ten: the four Vedas and the six Shastras; the eighteen: the eighteen Puranas.
24.1: The thirty and the five: the thirty fasts of Ramadan and the five daily prayers (namaz).
24.2: The measure (paaee): the pierced bowl of a water-clock, which fills and sinks to mark the time; here, the span of a life.
24.3: Dhaanak: a hunter, who goes about with dogs and a knife. The Guru speaks here in the voice of the erring human being; the dog is greed, the two she-dogs hope and craving.
25.3: The first line names no subject; the commentaries read it of Maya, whom no one can deceive, though she deceives others.
The Puranas are the eighteen ancient Hindu books of sacred lore.
27.1: The eighty-four lakh (8.4 million) forms of life: by tradition, all the kinds of being through which a soul passes from birth to birth.
The paaras is the stone said to turn iron to gold at its touch; here the paaras is the Guru.
27.2: Kasumbh, the safflower, gives a bright dye that soon fades.
29.2: Bairag: in Gurbani often a loving longing for the Lord, not only renunciation of the world; udasi: detachment from Maya.
Laag: the mordant a dyer gives cloth so that the colour holds fast; here the fear of God is that mordant.
30.2: The fourth state (turiya): the spiritual state beyond Maya's three qualities.
33.1: Trikuti (the knitted brow, 18.2) here is the hold of the three qualities.
To die while living (jeevat marai): while still living in the world, to die to self-conceit and its vices.
34.1: Satguru kiaa: kiaa here is the postposition of, not what; spurned by the True Guru.
34.2: The crane comes down on a ripe field and eats the crop; the commentators read it as old age or death, which falls on the field of life.
35.2: Paionu, chukaaianu: the ending -onu / -anu marks the doer as he (God): he put, he removed.
42.2: Thirty-three crore (330 million): the number of the gods in Puranic tradition. Saadhik (seekers): those striving for the perfection of the Siddhas.
43.2: A ghari is about twenty-four minutes, a muhat two gharis. In the harvest, the field is the world and the farmer God: at his order death takes the young, the grown and the old alike. Life is a night of four watches (pahar), and daybreak is death.
46.1: Naam, daan, isnaan: in Gurbani, meditating on the Naam, giving to others and pure living (cleansing) go together.
46.2: In the third stanza, ਰਹਾਉ is a verb, I remain, I live; it is not the shabad's Rahao (Pause).
48.3: The Shastras are the books of the six schools of Hindu philosophy; saun (shagun) is an omen, read as lucky or unlucky before an undertaking.
49.2: ਪਥੁ (Sanskrit pathya) is the diet a physician prescribes for an illness; here the Naam is that regimen for the disease of birth and death.
50.2: A goil is grassland by a river where herders bring their cattle to graze for a few days in a dry season; their stay there is brief.
50.3: In the first two stanzas the body is the bride and the soul her companion and husband; from the third, the soul is the bride and God the Husband.
The muklava is the rite by which a bride married young is later sent from her parents' home to her husband's.
52.2: The Paarjat (Parijata) is a tree of Indra's heaven which, in the Puranas, rose from the churning of the ocean and grants every wish.
53.1: Ashtapadi (ashta, eight; pad, stanza): a hymn of about eight stanzas.
Here ਨਾਈ is the Arabic sana, glory or praise (not ਨਾਉ, the Name); parvardigar (Persian) is the Sustainer.
Salik: one who travels the Sufi path; mashaikh: the great shaikhs (plural of shaikh); darood: the praise and blessing recited after the namaz.
53.2: The Tenth Gate (dasam duar): the inner door beyond the body's nine openings, where the soul meets God.
54.1: Majith (madder): a plant whose red dye never fades; in Gurbani, the image of lasting love.
57.1: Brahma is the creator god of the Puranas, from whose mouths the Vedas are held to have come; Vyas is the sage held to have arranged the Vedas and composed the Puranas.
58.1: In ਤੋੁਲਾਇਸੀ the letter ਤ carries two vowel signs (ੋ and ੁ); it is read tulaaisee, to keep the metre of the line.
59.1: Narad is a sage of the Puranas, messenger of the gods and a devotee of Vishnu.
59.2: The chatrik (pied cuckoo) is held in Indian poetry to drink only the raindrop that falls under the Swati star, and no other water; the chakvi (ruddy shelduck) is parted from her mate at night and waits all night for the sunrise.
Sohang (Sanskrit so'ham, he am I): the recognition that one's own self is of the light of the one Lord.
61.1: Thagauli: the stupefying herb (datura and the like) that thugs gave travellers in order to rob them.
Ashtadhatu: an alloy of eight metals; here the human body is the King's (God's) coin, minted in the Shabad, assayed, and taken into his treasury.
62.1: Some had their bodies sawn by the karvat (saw) at Kashi in the hope of liberation, and some ascetics went to melt their bodies in the Himalayan snows.
64.1: Mukaam (Persian maqam): a halt or lasting abode; a mulla's or fakir's mukaam is his seat (takia).
66.1: In this shabad the bird is the soul and the tree the body; the true feed it pecks is the Lord's Name.
67.1: Namdev was a chhimba, a calico printer, and Kabir a weaver; both were Bhagats of castes counted low, and the hymns of both are in the Guru Granth Sahib.
The demon's son is Prahlad, son of the demon king Harnakhash (Hiranyakashipu), who held to devotion to God through all his father's torments.

The six orders (khat darshan): the six sects of ascetics known by their garb, such as the yogis, jangams, sannyasis, bairagis, sarevras (Jains) and Buddhists; some read it as the six schools of Hindu philosophy.
70.1: The four great sins: the gravest sins of the Hindu law books; by one common count, killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, stealing gold and adultery with the teacher's wife.
The six rites (khat karam): the six duties of a Brahmin: studying and teaching the Vedas, performing and officiating at sacrifice, giving and receiving gifts.
71.1: The nine kinds of devotion (navadha bhakti), as the Vaishnavas count them: hearing of God, singing his praise, remembering him, serving his feet, worship, bowing down, servitude, friendship and offering up the self.
71.2: Each stanza of this hymn closes with ਜੀਉ (jeeo), a word of loving address that rounds off the line; it adds nothing to the sense.

The gopi (milkmaid), the river (Yamuna) and the cowherd recall the story of Krishna in Braj: all of them are God himself. ਗੋਇ is the earth; some read it as the hill Govardhan, which Krishna is said to have lifted.
73.1: The five rivals and the five young wrestlers are lust, anger, greed, attachment and pride; the five farmers who become tenants are the five senses, now under control.
A chhinjh is a village wrestling fair; the winning wrestler ties a turban with a high crest (dumala), and a pat on the back (thapi) is the mark of praise.
74.1: Pahare (the watches): the four watches of the night are the stages of a life. The mortal is a travelling merchant, come from the Lord's door to trade in the Name in this world, who spends one night here.
Kanh (Krishna) was raised as a child by Jasuda (Yashoda), wife of the cowherd Nand of Gokul, and was fondly passed from hand to hand.
78.1: Chhant: a song of longer stanzas. In this one the soul-bride speaks to her father (babul) as a daughter does at her wedding: the procession (janj), the dowry (daaj), the bridal clothes; the Husband is the Lord.
The bride's vine (vel) and the Guru's line (peerhee) are their descendants: all who, through them, come to meditate on the Name.
79.1: Banwari (he of the forest garland), Sri Rang and Sridhar (the lord of Sri, Lakshmi, and he who holds her) are names of Vishnu; in Gurbani they are names of God.
Chitr and Gupt are, by tradition, the two recorders at Dharam Raj's court who write down the deeds of every being.
The nine treasures (nau nidh): in Puranic lore, the nine treasures of Kuber, the god of wealth; here, every kind of wealth.
80.1: Dakhna: a salok in the speech of south-western Punjab (around Multan), where ਡ often stands for ਦ (ਡੂਜੜੋ, second) and ਹ for ਸ (ਹਭ, all).
Bikhai ban: here ban (Sanskrit vana) is water, set against the Amrit the devotees drink.
81.1: In this hymn (Vanjara, the merchant) each stanza is followed by its own two-line Rahao (Pause).
83.1: A vaar is a hymn of pauris (stanzas); in this vaar the pauris are the Fourth Guru's, and each pauri is preceded by saloks of the Gurus, the number after ਮਃ (Mahla) naming the Guru who wrote each one.
Apaaru (masculine, with aunkar) describes the Lord, not mati (understanding, feminine).
83.4: Sandeeaa: of, belonging to (a Lahndi genitive).
83.5: This salok is in Persian and Arabic words: sidak (faith), sabooree (contentment, thankfulness), saadik (the faithful), sabar (patience), tosaa (provisions for a journey), malaaik (angels), khaaik (idle talkers).
83.9: The fourteen shops: the fourteen worlds of Puranic count (seven above, seven below), which the Guru calls shops, where beings have come to trade (in the Name).
83.10: Shara and shariat: the religious law of Islam and its rules; sijda: the prostration of the namaz, the forehead to the ground; makhsood: aim, purpose.
84.2: The seven continents (deep), the seven seas and the nine regions (khand): the earth as the Puranas divide it.
85.2: Sebaal (Sanskrit shaivala): the green moss that forms on water.
87.2: Aatma deu, the Divine Self: God, who gives light to the soul; not a separate deity.
87.3: Liv is attention lovingly held on God; dhaat here is the mind's running after Maya. Sath: the village council where quarrels are settled.
88.4: Bhagauti: a Vaishnav who calls himself a devotee of Bhagavan (Vishnu).
88.6: Savaahee (Arabic sabah, morning) means at morning, not ashes; karr means fret, grieve.
91.1: Karee: the lines drawn round a cooking square (chauka) to keep it ritually pure. The touch of a dumni, a butcher woman, a sweeper woman or a chandal woman was held to defile it; the Guru names the vices within as what truly defiles.
91.2: The swan stands for the pure in mind, the crane for one who looks white but lies in wait for fish (the hypocrite), and the crow for the impure.
91.5: The eighteen siddhis: the miraculous powers of yoga, eight of them (anima, laghima and the rest) the best known.
91.6: A dhadhi is a bard who sings a patron's praise (a vaar) at his door and is rewarded with a robe of honour.
Sudh (corrected): written after the closing numbers of the vaar, it marks that the text was checked against the original.
91.7: Ek suaan: this hymn is sung in the ghar (musical setting) of Guru Nanak's Sri Raag hymn that begins ek suaan dui suaanee naal (Ang 24).
92.1: Beethal (Sanskrit Vitthala): a name of God; Trilochan uses it, like Narayan and Ramaiya, for the Lord who pervades forest and grass.
92.2: The image is a still: the furnace (bhaathee), its two pipes (singia and chungia) and the vat into which the distillate drips. Kabir makes the sky (the Tenth Gate) the furnace, a pure heart the golden vat, the nectar of the Name the distillate and the breath the cup.
93.1: This hymn is sung in the ghar (musical setting) of the Pahare, Guru Nanak's hymns in Sri Raag that tell a life through the four watches of the night (Ang 74).
94.1: Chaupade (chau, four; pad, stanza): hymns of four stanzas.
94.2: Madhusudan (the slayer of the demon Madhu): a name of Vishnu; in Gurbani, a name of God.
95.1: Narhari (nar, man; hari, lion): Narasimha, the Man-Lion in whose form, in the Puranas, God saved Prahlad; in Gurbani, a name of God.
97.3: Sabhraaee (sa, with; bhraa, brother): a bride with brothers, and so held in honour in her husband's home.
98.1: Nivli: a hatha yoga practice in which the belly muscles are rolled to cleanse the bowels; the eighty-four postures (asanas) are the sitting postures of hatha yoga.
98.2: Damodar (he whose waist was bound with a cord: the child Krishna) and Keshav (of the long, beautiful hair) are names of Vishnu and Krishna in the Puranas; in Gurbani they are names of the one God.
102.2: ਸੇ and ਨਿਰਬਾਣੇ are plural: those who stay untouched in the midst of all are the fortunate ones who have known God.
102.3: The meru is the head bead of a mala (a string of prayer beads), set above the others where the thread is knotted.
103.3: The akhara is the wrestling arena; bikhara (bikham akhara) is the hard bout. Drums of rejoicing sound for the victor.
104.1: In ਗੋੁਪਾਲਾ the letter ਗ carries two vowel signs (ੋ and ੁ); it is read gupaalaa, to keep the metre of the line.
106.3: Hathi: a palmful of medicine, as mothers place a dose of carom seed and the like on a child's palm.
108.1: The four padaarath: dharam (righteousness), arth (wealth), kaam (fulfilment of desire) and mokh (liberation), held to be the four aims of life.
108.3: The inverted lotus: the heart turned away from God, like a lotus hanging upside down and closed; turned towards him, it opens as the lotus does.
109.2: Hau vaari jeeo vaari: vaari is to be offered up in sacrifice; jeeo is the word of loving address (71.2), not the soul. In these ashtapadis the lines ending in -ania (vasaavania, suhaavania) mostly name those who do the act; in some lines the form reads as a plain verb.
113.1: The fourth step is the fourth state (turiya, 30.2).
In the game of chaupar the pieces move round the board to reach home; a piece that has reached home is ripe (pakki), one still out is raw (kachi).
117.1: Betaale: out of the beat (taal), as a singer loses the rhythm.
117.2: The slanderer is held to take on the sins of the one he slanders: he carries another's load and is paid nothing for it.
Vaasna is both a scent and the inclination placed within a being; vaasu is the fragrant one, the flower.
121.1: Naad: the sound the yogis raise on their horn (singi); here the praise of the True One is that sound.
121.2: Dancing in a marked-out ring (pirr): troupes of the raas marked out a ring and, dancing to rhythm and instruments, enacted the life of Krishna and called it devotion; the hymn's dance, beat and instruments allude to it.
126.2: Ihu (with -u, masculine) is the soul, not the cave (gufa is feminine): through the Guru's Shabad the soul reflects on the cave of the body.
128.2: Nihkarmi: free of the bond of deeds; not one who does nothing, but one who acts without Haumai and desire, so that his deeds do not bind him.
The lake and the swan: in Indian poetry the swan lives on the lake Mansarovar and feeds on pearls; here the lake is the Lord and the swans are his Saints.
132.2: Tapavas (Arabic): judgement, justice. A moora is the hide of a dead calf stuffed with straw and set before a cow or buffalo so that she gives milk: alive to look at, dead within.
133.1: Barah Maha (the twelve months): a song of the year in which each month's season voices the soul-bride's longing for her Husband Lord. This one opens with a prayer, and its months run from Chet (mid-March to mid-April).
134.4: Pret: one who has died; as soon as the life leaves it, the body is called pret, held unclean and carried out of the house in haste.
135.3: In ਸੋੁਹੰਦਾ the letter ਸ carries two vowel signs (ੋ and ੁ); it is read suhanda, to keep the metre of the line.
135.4: On the first day of Magh (Maghi) a bath at a tirath such as Prayag was held to bring great merit.
136.3: Din Raini (day and night) is the title of this bani of four stanzas; the words recur in its lines.
Manj: my, of me (a Lahndi form); manj nimani thaau, the refuge of me, the humble one.
137.1: Malak Murid and Chandrahara Sohia: by tradition, two chiefs of Akbar's time (of the Malak and Sohi clans) whose fight the bards sang as a vaar; this vaar is to be sung to its tune (dhuni).
137.2: Patal: a plate of leaves. In the shraadh rites for the dead, food is set out on leaf-plates and the crows are called to it, in the belief that it reaches the departed.
139.1: Seeing without eyes and the rest: the senses held back from their pull to vice, so that one lives in the world dead to it.
139.4: The mountain of gold: Sumer (Meru), the golden mountain at the centre of the world in the Puranas. In old tradition each of the four Vedas has its colour: the Sama white, the Rig red, the Yajur yellow, the Atharva black.
140.3: Paleet (Persian palid): unclean; a garment stained with blood is held unfit for the namaz.
140.6: Musalla: the prayer mat; sunnat: circumcision; roza: the fast; the Kaaba: the shrine at Mecca towards which Muslims pray; Pir: a spiritual guide; kalma: the declaration of faith; tasbi: the rosary.
141.1: Halal and haram: what Islamic law allows and what it forbids. Pork is forbidden to the Muslim, and the cow is sacred to the Hindu.
141.4: Maskal (miskala): the burnisher that scrapes the rust off a blade; so, giving his possessions away, he scrapes off the rust of pride in them.
141.6: Sikdar: a chief; taji: a horse of Arab breed; tukhar: a camel; pakhar: the howdah and trappings of an elephant; saraiche: the screens round a tent; lalti: of red satin; sinakhat (Persian): recognition.
142.1: The eighteen loads: all plant life; an old belief holds that one leaf of every kind of tree and plant, weighed together, comes to eighteen bhaar (an old measure of weight).
142.2: Rahu and Ketu: two ill-omened planets of astrology; in the Puranic story they are the demons who eclipse the sun and the moon.
142.4: This pauri uses Persian and Arabic words: badfaili (evil deed), gaibaana (in secret), devaana (mad), kufr (falsehood, denial of God), subhaan (glorious, wondrous), deevaan (court).
142.7: Tabalbaaj: an army's drummer, who beats out the order to march; saakhti (Persian): saddling and harnessing a horse; taakhti: a gallop.
142.8: At the door: at the mill's central opening, by the pivot; grains that stay there are not ground between the stones.
142.9: Patreeai is a verb, one is brought to ruin; mithai: because of sweetness (not the sweet-leaved cane).
143.2: Taaroo: water so deep it can only be crossed by swimming; maaran: reducing a metal to calx (kushta) by fire.
143.5: This salok is in Persian: ham (hama, all), jer jimi (beneath the earth), masaaik (sheikhs), me ravad (goes, passes away), afjoo (afzun, ever increasing).
143.6: Asti ek digar kui (Persian): One alone is; who is the other? Ek tui: you alone.
144.1: Daade dihand (Persian daad dihand): givers of justice.
144.3: Persian words: dast (hand), aa kase (of anyone), hamaa raa (for all), vase (bas, enough).
144.4: Persian words: parandae (birds), giraah (knot), jar (gold, wealth), darakhat (trees), aab (water).
144.7: Charg and kuhi: hunting birds of the hawk kind; giraah: a morsel, daily bread.
147.5: Hansu here is hinsa, cruelty, not the swan.
148.4: Savaareeaas: the ending -aas marks the doer as he (God): she whom he has adorned.
148.6: The first two lines are in Sahaskriti, a Sanskrit-coloured idiom: tasi (tasya), of him; janamasi, (his) birth is; jaavatu (yaavat), so long as. Ke means many, for the verb tarahi is plural.
149.1: Paahee (Sanskrit upaanah): shoes; to be beaten with shoes is the punishment of disgrace.
149.7: This salok is about the Jain monks of the time (sarevre), who, for fear of harming the smallest living being, had their hair plucked out, neither bathed nor drank fresh water, and walked in single file sweeping the path with a whisk.

Pind, pattal, kiria and deeva are Hindu rites for the dead: balls of rice offered to the departed, food on leaf-plates, the rites after death, and the lamp lit in their name. Jangams are Shaiva mendicants who go about ringing bells.
151.1: Raag Gauri is sung in several forms, and the heading of each hymn names its form: Gauri Guareri, Cheti, Bairagan, Poorbi, Dakhani, Majh, Mala and others. Dupade (du, two; pad, stanza): hymns of two stanzas.
Sacha here is saancha, the mould into which metal is cast, not sacha, true; sat is the hammer's stroke that stamps it. The image is the minting of a coin, as in the 38th pauri of Japji Sahib.
154.3: The three states (avastha): in the Vedanta's count, waking, dreaming and deep sleep (some read them as the mind's states under the three qualities); the fourth state is turiya (30.2).
154.4: In this shabad the soul speaks, now to the body (kaaia), now to itself (jeearre); in the second Rahao the body speaks.
Lanka of gold: the city of Ravan in the Ramayana; its golden palaces did not stay his.
155.2: Raval: a yogi of Gorakhnath's order. The yogi's garb is named here: the large earrings (mundra), the patched coat (khintha), the staff (danda), and roots and tubers (kand mool) for food.
The ਤਾ at the end of ਖਿੰਥਾਤਾ, ਪਾਵਸਿਤਾ and the rest only fills out the tune; it adds nothing to the sense.
160.3: Kalyug here is a state of the mind more than an age: it is born in the heart of the chandal, the doer of evil.
162.2: The image: the water hidden in the earth and the water the clouds rain down are one water; so all forms are the one Lord's.
163.2: Gorakh (Gorakhnath): the teacher revered by the Nath yogis.
Brahmin, Khatri (Kshatriya), Vaish and Shudra are the four varnas: by the Shastras the Khatri's duty is war, the Vaish's trade and farming, and the Shudra's the service of the other three.
164.2: Preet in this hymn and the next is the delight love takes in what it loves (Sanskrit priti: pleasure, joy, affection).
165.1: Balbhadra (Balram) was Krishna's elder brother; by the Puranas both studied under the sage Sandipani and served him as their guru.
165.4: Twenty-one generations (ikih kul): an old way of saying a person's whole line, the generations before and after.
167.1: Mat here means perhaps, in the hope that; it is not mat(i), the intellect.
168.3: The go-between (vichola) arranges a marriage and brings the bride to the bridegroom; the Guru unites the soul-bride with the Lord.
171.2: Garur: a remedy against snake venom, named after Garuda, the bird who is the enemy of snakes; it was ground on a stone and taken by mouth.
172.3: Sawan (mid-July to mid-August) is the month of the monsoon rains, when the peacock cries out with joy at the sight of the clouds.
173.1: Kaaman: the charms a woman was believed to use to win her husband's love; here the virtues are those charms.
175.3: Rahao Dooja: the second Rahao (Pause) of this shabad, which answers the question asked in the first.
176.2: Brikh here is the ox (Sanskrit vrisha), not a tree; like the horse, it is yoked.
180.3: The Shah here is the banker who gives traders capital on credit (visah): God is the Banker, the soul a trader in the Name, and the Guru its surety.
185.3: Sati: a widow who burned herself on her husband's funeral pyre, a custom of the time; the word also means a woman true in conduct, the sense of the last line.
185.4: The treasure of father and grandfather: the commentators take it to be the Bani of the Gurus before Guru Arjan Dev Ji, which came down to him as his inheritance.
188.3: This shabad is spoken to one who is wailing over the death of a relative.
192.1: Gur murat: the Guru's form; in Gurbani this is the Guru's Shabad (Bhai Gurdas: the Guru's form is the Guru's Word), not a picture or an idol.
197.1: Bathing at a place of pilgrimage and giving alms at an eclipse of the sun or moon was held to earn very great merit.
199.1: Baisno (Vaishnav): a worshipper of Vishnu, who keeps rules of purity, fasts and worship; here the name is given to the one whose love is with God and who has given up the vices.
200.3: Sitala is smallpox, which people took to be the wrath of the goddess Sitala.
203.3: Rahoa (plural rahoe): a Punjabi folk song sung with a long-drawn call, chiefly by women at weddings; this hymn is to be sung in the ghar (tune) of their chhants.
Sanak and his brothers: Sanak, Sanandan, Sanatan and Sanat Kumar, in the Puranas the four sons of Brahma, sages held to remain children for ever.
205.1: Raghurai: the king of the line of Raghu, Rama; in Gurbani, a name of the one God.
207.1: Shiv here means the auspicious One, the giver of good, not the god Shiva.
208.1: Each line takes an item of the yogi's garb and discipline (earrings, ashes, the sect, the food of his order, the seat, the horn, the staff) and gives its inner form. The five disciples are the five senses; the ten are the five senses and the five organs of action.
208.3: The chakor: a bird said in Indian lore to gaze at the moon all night long.
210.4: Diwan: a high officer of a ruler's court, in whose service men worked for pay; the hymn is a picture of service: chaakar (servant), vajahu (wages) and bakhsees (reward).
211.5: Raj Jog: kingship and yoga together, union with God while living the householder's life.
212.5: Chintamani: the jewel that, by tradition, grants whatever is wished for in the mind.
212.6: An elephant, once bathed, throws dust over itself again.
213.3: The staff-bearers (dandi) are sannyasis who carry a staff. Ho in this hymn is a call (O brother) that also fills out the tune.
214.1: Pocha: the wet cloth or plaster laid on the pipe of a still to keep it cool, so that the vapour condenses and drips.
214.2: Shivpuri, Brahmpuri, Indrapuri: the heavens of Shiv, Brahma and Indra, which the Puranas promise as the reward of fire offerings, sacrifices and pilgrimages.
216.1: Robbed on this side: as a traveller's goods are plundered on the road, these deeds are lost before they reach the Lord's court. Aadh: half a cowrie shell, the smallest of values.
219.5: Gaj: in the Bhagavat Purana, an elephant (Gajendra) seized in the water by a crocodile; when his strength failed he called on the Lord and was set free.
