223.1: The two paths: in the commentaries, the Guru's way and the way of the self-willed mind; Gurbani elsewhere names them liv and dhaat, attunement to God and running after Maya.
223.2: Sun and moon: heat and cold, harsh treatment and kind alike; to the yogis the words also name the right and left breath channels (pingala and ida).
224.2: Brahma: by the Puranic story, a demon carried off the Vedas while Brahma slept, and they were restored only when he turned to God.

Bali: a demon king who held sacrifices to win Indra's throne; heedless of his guru Shukra's warning, he granted Vishnu, come as the dwarf Vaman, the land of three steps, and was sent down to the netherworld. Harichand (Harishchandra): a king famed for truth and giving, who, put to the test by the sage Vishvamitra, gave away his kingdom and was sold into servitude.

Sahasbahu (the thousand-armed king), Madhu and Kaitabh, Mahikhasur, Jarasandh, Kalyavan, Raktabij and Kalnem: proud kings and demons of the Puranas, slain by Parashuram, Vishnu and Durga, or through Krishna (Jarasandh by Bhim at his side).

Duryodhan: the eldest of the Kauravas in the Mahabharata, slain in the war with the Pandavas. Janmejay: Parikshit's son, who by tradition set aside the counsel of his guru Vyas and was struck with leprosy. Kans, Krishna's uncle, and Keshi and Chandur, his champions, were slain by Krishna.
225.2: Each of these creatures dies through one sense: the bumble-bee through smell, shut in the closing lotus; the moth through sight, in the flame; the elephant through touch, lured into a pit by a she-elephant; the fish through taste, on the bait; the deer through hearing, drawn by the hunter's music.
227.1: By the Puranic story, Brahma was born on a lotus that grew from Vishnu's navel; to find its root he went down its stalk into the netherworld, and could not reach its end.
227.2: Param Hans (the supreme swan): of old, the name of a renunciant of the highest order; the swan is held to separate milk from water. Here it is the one whose food is the Naam.
229.2: Sutak: in Hindu custom, the impurity held to fall on a household for some days after a birth (or a death), during which no worship or rites are performed. The Guru uses the word for the mind's impurity, the love of another.
229.3: The daughter of the ocean: in the Puranas, Lakshmi, goddess of wealth, rose when the gods and demons churned the ocean; here, Maya.
231.1: Seedhe (sijhe): succeeded, their life brought to fulfilment; reedhe: delighted, won over.
234.1: Karhala: a camel (Sanskrit karabha). The mind is likened to the camel that roams foreign lands under its load, ever far from its home; from it these two hymns are named Karhale.
237.1: Dhoti here is the yogis' cleansing (neti-dhoti): a strip of cloth swallowed to clean the stomach; hoti (hotri) is the priest who performs the fire offering.
237.2: Dubidha (duality): the divided mind, which sees mine and yours and loves another besides God; in every line, isu (this) is this duality.
239.3: Akal: without parts (kala), the One who neither wanes nor waxes as the moon does; a name of God.
242.1: Jumla (the total): the closing figure 44 is the count of all the Ashtapadis in Raag Gauri.
242.2: Milk once drawn does not come back to the teats: the youth (and the chance of union) lost in pride do not return.
The friends and the wicked: in the commentaries, the virtues within, which flourish, and the vices, which are crushed.
246.1: In this hymn a wife speaks to her husband, who leaves home to serve another in foreign lands; in the commentaries this husband is the soul, which leaves its home within to wander after Maya.
The closing figure 7 is the total of these Chhants in Raag Gauri: two by the First Guru and five by the Third.
250.1: Bavan Akhri (fifty-two letters): a composition in which each pauri opens with a letter of the alphabet (Ong, Sassa, Dhadha, Nganga and the rest); each salok gives the thought that the pauri after it unfolds.
250.3: Ong: the first letter of the alphabet, here also the name of Ik Oankar, the One God. Sunn (the void): the state before creation, when there was nothing but God.
250.4: Nirgun: God beyond the three qualities of Maya; Sargun: God made manifest in the creation, with its qualities.
251.3: Nganga: for the acrostic, giaan (spiritual wisdom) and giaani (the wise) are spelt here with the letter ਙ.
253.5: Purak, kumbhak and rechak are the three parts of the yogis' breath control (pranayam). A sompaak cooks his own food for ritual purity; an aparas lets no one touch him.
254.4: Punahcharan: a rite of expiation, performed to wipe out the effect of a sin.
254.7: In ਗੋੁਬਿੰਦ the letter ਗ carries two vowel signs (ੋ and ੁ); it is read gubind, to keep the metre of the line.
255.2: The nalini is a parrot trap: a reed that turns on a rod set over a bowl of water, with grain on it. When the parrot perches, the reed turns over; seeing the water below, the frightened bird clings to it and so is caught by its own hold.
259.9: Vasudev: a name of Krishna, son of Vasudeva; in Gurbani it names God, who dwells in all.
261.6: Akhar: in this pauri, letters, the written and spoken word in which the whole visible world is named and known; in the salok before it, akhar (Sanskrit akshara, the imperishable) is the imperishable Lord, who is untouched by letters.
296.1: Thiti (lunar days): the days of the moon's fortnight, Ekam (the first), Dutiya (the second), Tritiya (the third) and the rest. Each pauri of this bani opens with a lunar day's name, and instead of the day's observances the Guru draws a teaching from the name (Ekam: the One Creator; Dutiya: duality and evil-mindedness; Tritiya: the three qualities).
297.8: Sekh: Shesh Nag, the thousand-headed serpent of the Puranas, held to utter a new Name of God with every tongue. Suk (Shukdev), the son of the sage Vyas, recited the Bhagavat Purana to King Parikshit.
299.2: On Ekadasi, the eleventh day of the moon's fortnight, many Hindus fast from grain; here the Guru tells what the true fast is.
299.4: Panch bhoo atma: the mind, held to be formed from the subtle part of the five elements (earth, water, fire, air and ether).
299.6: The three fevers: adhi (ills of the mind), biadhi (ills of the body) and upadhi (troubles and calamities that come from without).
302.3: Jaani, bhaani, ajaani, vakhaani and samaani are feminine: this pauri speaks of the soul-bride.
305.4: Amrit sar, the pool of Amrit: in Gurbani, the Naam pictured as a pool of Amrit; after the outward bath, the Sikh dips in it.
306.2: This salok tells of an incident: by tradition, a man turned away from the Guru, with his servant, brought false complaints against Guru Amar Das Ji before the emperor Akbar, and both came back disgraced.
309.1: Bahi tikia: (the Guru) sat and anointed (him) with the tilak, that is, himself entrusted (him) with the Guruship.
315.3: Azrail (Azrael): in Islamic tradition, the angel of death, who takes the soul from the body.
315.10: This salok tells of an incident: by tradition, an ascetic (tapa) first turned down the Guru's invitation to receive the alms given to holy men, then, greedy for the large offering, seated his own son among them (to take a share). Panch: the leading men of the town, its council.
318.1: Rai Kamaldi Mojdi: by tradition, Rai Kamaluddin and his nephew Maujuddin, whose fight the bards sang as a vaar; this vaar is to be sung to its tune (dhuni).
319.9: The pods of the ak split open when they dry, and scatter in a thousand silky tufts.
319.11: Nanaku, with the aunkar, is the subject here: it is Nanak, the Guru, who gives the Name; it is not an address (O Nanak).
319.13: This salok speaks to a Muslim in his own terms: Dozakh is hell, and Rasul is God's Prophet, who here stands for the Guru.
321.1: Bhaleria here means bad, evil, not good.
321.11: The commentaries read this salok as an image of the rain of the Name: the earth is the heart, and the grain the Lord's praise.
322.3: The kite: in the commentaries, the mind cut off from God, which roams everywhere yet settles only on the carrion of vice.
322.5: Doha: a couplet, a metre of two lines.
322.9: Khundi: a game played with a curved stick and a ball; kunde: the butts of guns.
323.5: Jajman: the patron whose household rites a Brahmin performs and who gives him his dues.
325.5: The little well is the body (and attachment to it), the five water-drawers are the senses, and the broken rope is the want of true understanding: the misled intellect labours through the senses to draw pleasure, and gets nothing (the Darpan's reading).
326.1: By the Darpan's reading, the last stanza (ਰਾਮ ਰਮਤ ਮਤਿ ਪਰਗਟੀ ਆਈ …) is the Fifth Guru's, joined to tell how this understanding comes; the extra figure 1 in the closing numbers marks it. The Faridkot Teeka takes the whole hymn as the Guru's.

In the Darpan's reading, the donkey and the maddened buffalo are the foolish, headstrong mind feeding on pleasures; the ewe suckling at her lamb is the intellect following the mind, when the mind should follow the intellect.
326.2: Panchpade: hymns of five stanzas. Kashi (Banaras), Shiva's city, was believed to free whoever died there, and Magahar to send whoever died there into birth as a donkey; to break this belief, Kabir left Kashi in old age to live and die at Magahar.
326.4: Tipade Chartuke: hymns of three stanzas, each of four lines.
327.1: Sukhmana: in yoga, the central channel of the subtle body, between the ida and the pingala, where yogis hold the breath; the ida and the pingala they also call the Ganga and the Jamuna, whose meeting, like the Triveni at Prayag, counts as a holy bathing place. Kabir turns these images inward; the Darpan reads the Rahao line as remembering the Name with every breath.
328.6: Kabir speaks of the Name's elixir in the image of distilling: the still, the firewood and the kalalan (the woman who serves the wine); the sky is the raised mind where the elixir drips.
329.2: The Smritis: the law-books based on the Vedas (Manu's and others), which lay down the rules of caste and ritual.
329.4: The five ambrosial foods: milk, curd, ghee, sugar and honey, held to be the finest of foods.
329.5: Nat: the player who takes on every part of his show himself.
330.1: Pade: hymns; thirty-five is the count of Kabir's hymns in Gauri Guareri up to here.
330.4: This hymn is to be sung both in Raag Gauri and in Raag Sorath.
331.1: Thagauri (the thugs' stupefying drug, 61.1) here is the attachment by which the Lord holds the world spellbound.
332.1: By the Puranic story, King Bhagirath brought the Ganga down from heaven to the earth.
332.2: Shraadh: the rite for dead forebears (pitars), in which food is given to Brahmins and set out for crows, in the belief that it reaches the forebears.
Akul: without kul (lineage); the Lord, who has no forebears.
333.1: The six chakras: in yoga, six centres in the body, from the base of the spine to the point between the brows, through which yogis draw the breath upward.
Palita: the fuse that fires the powder of a gun.
333.3: Tanda: a trader's caravan of laden oxen; nayak: the master of the banjaras (travelling traders); jagati: the collector of tolls on the road.
334.3: Kingri: the yogis' stringed instrument, a stem set on two gourds; batua: the yogi's pouch for ashes; tari: the yogic trance.
335.1: The body here is cloth on a loom: the commentators read the nine yards as the body's nine openings, the ten as the senses, the twenty-one as the elements, the vital airs and the mind, the sixty threads as the main channels of the body, the nine pieces as its joints and the seventy-two as its finer channels.

Maho: the mind's craving, which takes the soul off again and again to have a body woven; sizing (pachan): the paste that stiffens the warp, here the daily food; the troughs (kunde): the pots in which the bobbins are kept soaking; the beam (tur): the roller on which the woven cloth is wound.
335.2: Kashi: by the Puranas, Shiva whispers the saving mantra (the Name of Ram) into the ear of one who dies in Kashi (Benares), and he is liberated.
335.4: A monkey is trapped with grain put in a narrow-mouthed pot: the full fist will not come out, and the greedy monkey will not let go, so he is caught, and the showman makes him dance from door to door.
Nalini: a parrot trap, a turning tube baited with grain over water; when the parrot perches, the tube turns over, and in fear of falling he clings to it and is caught.
336.2: Tin ko mandar: tin is straw or grass; the body is a house of straw, set alight by the fire of passing life.
337.1: Dhru: the child prince who, slighted by his stepmother, gave himself to devotion and was given an unmoving place as the Pole Star.
337.2: It was believed that the child in the womb, hanging head down like an ascetic doing penance upside down, remembers God.
337.5: A woman awaiting her husband from abroad shoos the crow from the roof: if it flies off, her beloved is said to be coming. In udahu na, the na is not a negative but a fond entreaty.
338.1: Kabir takes the longing of the milkmaid of Gokul, enchanted by Krishna in Brindaban, as the picture of his own love for the Lord.
338.3: Sindhaura: the coconut smeared with vermilion that a widow took in her hand as she went to be burned on her husband's pyre; once she had taken it, there was no turning back.
338.5: Nand: the cowherd of Gokul in whose home, by the Puranas, Krishna was brought up; Kabir answers the belief that God was born as anyone's son.
340.5: Tariqat: the second of the four stages of the Sufi path to God (shariat, tariqat, marifat, haqiqat), the stage of the heart's purification.
340.7: The lotus opens to the sun's ray and closes when the moon rises.
342.4: Shakti and Shiv: in Hindu thought the Goddess (the power of Maya) and Shiv; the Darpan and the Faridkot Teeka read that the mind becomes what it joins: Maya with Maya, the Lord with the Lord, the body with the body. Unman: the state of the mind raised above the world's thoughts and settled in the Lord.
342.8: Bisan (Vishnu) is here a name of the one Lord; the Bisantana, the son of Bisan, is his devotee, who like a child knows him alone as his keeper.
343.10: Khat chakra (the six wheels): taking the name of the yogis' six chakras, here, by the Darpan and the Faridkot Teeka, the five senses and the mind; the six directions are the four quarters, below and above.
343.12: The eight elements (dhatu): in the old count, the eight constituents of the body (by the Darpan: chyle, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, semen and the nerves).
344.3: Twelve suns: the Puranas count twelve suns (the Adityas); here they are the full light of knowledge risen within.
344.7: Vaar Sat (the seven days): each stanza opens with a day of the week: Aadit (Sunday), Somvar (Monday), Mangalvar (Tuesday), Budhvar (Wednesday), Brihaspati (Thursday) and Thavar (Saturday); Friday's (Shukarvar's) stanza opens with the like-sounding sukrit, good deeds. In place of each day's fasts and observances, Kabir draws a lesson in devotion from its name.

The upturned lotus: the heart turned away from the Lord. Trikuti (the knitted brow, 18.2) the Darpan reads as the mind's fretting; yogis give the name trikuti to the point between the brows, where the ida, pingala and sukhmana are held to meet, and the Faridkot Teeka and the Santhya read the line as bathing there day and night in that inner Triveni to wash away sins.
345.1: Stones: the stones of Ram's bridge to Lanka, said to have floated because his Name was written on them.

Ganika: a courtesan, saved by teaching a parrot to say Ram; Kubija: the hunchbacked maid of Kans, made straight and fair by Krishna; Ajamal: a fallen Brahmin, saved when at death he called his son Narayan; the hunter: Jara, who shot Krishna in the foot, taking him for a deer.
Bidar (Vidura): born of a maidservant, a devotee of Krishna; Sudama: Krishna's poor Brahmin friend, made rich by him; Ugrasain: the father of Kans, restored to the throne when Krishna slew Kans.
345.2: Begampura (be-gham, without sorrow): the city is the soul's own state in union with the Lord, reached in this life, set against the heaven that others promise after death.
345.3: The trader is the seeker: his ox is the mind, his capital and cargo the Lord's Name, and the hard mountain passes the lures of the senses on the way.
The knowers of this world and the next: Chitr and Gupt, who write down each one's deeds for Jam.
346.2: Satjug, Treta, Duapar and Kalyug: the four ages of the Puranic count; the scriptures give each age its own way to liberation, which Ravidas questions here.
